claims.text: The material proposed for lattice heat-conductivity control is single-crystalline silicon.
Introducing SRO precipitates into single-crystalline silicon reduces its lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine silicon.
SRO precipitates act as additional phonon-scattering centers in silicon.
The initial material is pristine single-crystalline silicon with minimal defects and no SRO precipitates.
Controlled doping and thermal annealing can induce SRO precipitate formation in single-crystalline silicon.
At the proposed experimental conditions, such as room temperature, phonons dominate thermal conduction in the silicon samples.
Electronic contributions to thermal conduction are minimal under the proposed conditions.
The intervention produces nanometer-scale SRO precipitates dispersed within the silicon lattice.
Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates reduces phonon lifetimes or scattering times.
Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates reduces phonon mean free paths.
Reduced phonon lifetimes and mean free paths decrease lattice thermal conductivity.
Silicon samples containing induced SRO precipitates will exhibit a measurable decrease in lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine single-crystalline silicon controls.
Pristine defect-free single-crystalline silicon has high lattice thermal conductivity because of long phonon mean free paths.
The proposed effect applies only in temperature regimes where phonon conduction is dominant.
The proposed effect is limited to precipitate concentrations that do not compromise the overall crystal structure.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction likely depends on SRO precipitate size, density, and distribution.
